I. $Q$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Q$ shown above. Find the matrix $R$ such that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of $A.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133821 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3a08d141-4335-56a2-8562-7ce4a6f3683b" "question-e5f7e59e-edf4-549f-aea0-27ed8989142e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133633 :question/problem "![](images/db/db19bfb8029513dcb3dc109a0752f87ecf405a6aa56881849f553d30fa1085ff.svg)

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above, where $\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \big\}$ is an orthogonal set of vectors. You're given that $\Vert\mathbf{v}_1\Vert =2,$ $\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert =3,$ $\Vert\mathbf{v}_3\Vert =4,$ and that the system of equations below describes the relationship between the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}={a}_{1} \\ {v}_{2}={a}_{2}-{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{3}={a}_{3}-3{v}_{1}+2{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the value of $r_{13}+r_{23}+r_{33}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we normalize the vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{2}\,⟹\,{v}_{1}=2{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{3}\,⟹\,{v}_{2}=3{q}_{2} \\ {q}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{4}\,⟹\,{v}_{3}=4{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the set $\big\{ \mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2,\mathbf{q}_3 \big\}$ will be both orthogonal and normalized.

Next, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$

![](images/f5/f53a5eb3b2d24ad186382f8eed42775b2ee61d34a20a0af821a38c17d846e873.svg)

The final system can be written in matrix form as follows:
![](images/27/2797cd9e375b3a28f3f8afc8c49b85e202ad5cc87fb5a332ebb9abd73f388ee3.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
r_{13}+r_{23}+r_{33} = 6+(-6)+4 = 4.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133863 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-946d71c0-c7c2-59d9-aaa7-5ecb48201289"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133679 :question/problem "![](images/12/128c3de38ca9c80e3e0d22d939fe05c88404fed97dee1a94f59aff5331f56172.svg)

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ of $A$ are orthogonal, and that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained by normalizing the columns of $A,$ what is the value of $q_{12} \cdot r_{22}?$" :question/worked-solution "Since the columns of $A$ are already orthogonal, to construct a matrix $Q,$ we simply normalize $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2\mathbf{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{‖{a}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{‖{a}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

![](images/5d/5d8b0271c6dcd970ec7c8d652433a798daf97e67792c47db1f6eef4bd39ad651.svg)

Finally, $q_{12} \cdot r_{22} = -\dfrac{2}{3} \cdot 3 = -2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133798 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8825d6b3-93be-5a03-9cc7-5000a40034aa"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133607 :question/problem "![](images/8d/8d29d0f5dd5e0d2c79c8d2c40c49b358a01dc5bb5536153fe05068773ef1e228.svg)

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of $q_{11} \cdot r_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ![](images/71/714ad80d47ea58159e0e486f5bfc5a6657fd441bc47aa2b8fa7230a89bdb0445.svg)

**Step 2**. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-\frac{12}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

![](images/a6/a6377dfb1e7ed7afafe348354dd21b2195c12495d9a5a6dcd98fec3aaeb8162d.svg)

Finally, $q_{11} \cdot r_{12} = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\right) \cdot \left({2\sqrt6}\right) = 2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186363203 :question/problem "Given that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of a $5\times 4$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, which of the following statements are true?

I. The columns of $Q$ are orthogonal

II. $Q$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix

III. $R$ is a  square  matrix" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5b19eecb-3ecc-5584-a617-4bf8675e0b01" :question/id #uuid "5b19eecb-3ecc-5584-a617-4bf8675e0b01" :question/math-academy-id "q-95917" :question/problem "Given that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of a $4\times 2$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, which of the following statements are true?

I. $Q$ is a $4\times 2$ upper triangular matrix

II. The columns of $Q$ are unit vectors

III. $R$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ then

$$
{A}_{m\times n}={Q}_{m\times n}\times {R}_{n\times n},
$$

where 

- $Q$ is an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)$

- $R$ is an $n\times n$ upper triangular matrix

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. $Q$ should be a $4\times 2$ matrix, but is not necessarily upper triangular.

- Statement II is true. Since the columns of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis, they are unit vectors.

- Statement III is false. $R$ must be a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-77a7384a-2954-50d8-86d9-02fc2c11bedd"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Given that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of an $8\times 4$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, which of the following statements are true?

I. $Q$ is an $8\times 4$ matrix

II. $R$ is an $8\times 8$ matrix

III. $R$ is an upper triangular matrix" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $A=QR$ is a  QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ then

$$
{A}_{m\times n}={Q}_{m\times n}\times {R}_{n\times n},
$$

where 

- $Q$ is an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)$

- $R$ is an $n\times n$ upper triangular matrix

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $Q$ must be an $8\times 4$ matrix.

- Statement II is false. $R$ should be a $4\times 4$ matrix.

- Statement III is true. Indeed $R$ must be an upper triangular matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-16d9df2f-7dae-571c-9898-8b25f88afb03"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-16d9df2f-7dae-571c-9898-8b25f88afb03" :answer-field/id #uuid "16d9df2f-7dae-571c-9898-8b25f88afb03" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ee9fd3db-d080-510c-8cba-0c10cffe8599" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f0b12155-382a-5236-96d0-5241fdc65d8e" "answer-ee9fd3db-d080-510c-8cba-0c10cffe8599" "answer-c4b65933-5b0f-5c15-a729-3b530d4943b2" "answer-b3c6518b-cfa4-5881-b743-5099d5ac42c2" "answer-34dee133-5da2-587d-bf0e-88da035eca52"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f0b12155-382a-5236-96d0-5241fdc65d8e" :answer/id #uuid "f0b12155-382a-5236-96d0-5241fdc65d8e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee9fd3db-d080-510c-8cba-0c10cffe8599" :answer/id #uuid "ee9fd3db-d080-510c-8cba-0c10cffe8599" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4b65933-5b0f-5c15-a729-3b530d4943b2" :answer/id #uuid "c4b65933-5b0f-5c15-a729-3b530d4943b2" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b3c6518b-cfa4-5881-b743-5099d5ac42c2" :answer/id #uuid "b3c6518b-cfa4-5881-b743-5099d5ac42c2" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-34dee133-5da2-587d-bf0e-88da035eca52" :answer/id #uuid "34dee133-5da2-587d-bf0e-88da035eca52" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186364571 :question/problem "Given that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, which of the following statements are true?

I. The columns of $Q$ are orthonormal

II. $Q$ is a square matrix

III. $R$ is a square matrix" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-71004f41-ae2f-50fd-9fdc-88ec92c18337" :question/id #uuid "71004f41-ae2f-50fd-9fdc-88ec92c18337" :question/math-academy-id "q-95919" :question/problem "Given that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of a $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, which of the following statements are true?

I. $Q$ is a square matrix

II. $\text{Col}(A)$ is spanned by the columns of $Q$

III. $R$ is a square matrix" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ then

$$
{A}_{m\times n}={Q}_{m\times n}\times {R}_{n\times n},
$$

where 

- $Q$ is an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)$

- $R$ is an $n\times n$ upper triangular matrix

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. $Q$ should be an $m\times n$ matrix, so $Q$ is not necessarily a square matrix.

- Statement II is true.  Since the columns of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A),$ they must span $\text{Col}(A).$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, $R$ must be an $m\times n$ matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7fd0a920-47da-5738-85dc-fcfde1071d1a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7fd0a920-47da-5738-85dc-fcfde1071d1a" :answer-field/id #uuid "7fd0a920-47da-5738-85dc-fcfde1071d1a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3108f868-6810-5414-b79d-ed9c59cf14cc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-30cd0132-8138-5a90-bf6d-84623e148b9a" "answer-1194f3e3-1844-5ab9-9daf-5533b0a96a9d" "answer-62bcf903-0255-59aa-affe-9d6ade55eb53" "answer-3108f868-6810-5414-b79d-ed9c59cf14cc" "answer-eede4f00-fcca-5952-bf0b-1b45f39cc595"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-30cd0132-8138-5a90-bf6d-84623e148b9a" :answer/id #uuid "30cd0132-8138-5a90-bf6d-84623e148b9a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1194f3e3-1844-5ab9-9daf-5533b0a96a9d" :answer/id #uuid "1194f3e3-1844-5ab9-9daf-5533b0a96a9d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-62bcf903-0255-59aa-affe-9d6ade55eb53" :answer/id #uuid "62bcf903-0255-59aa-affe-9d6ade55eb53" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3108f868-6810-5414-b79d-ed9c59cf14cc" :answer/id #uuid "3108f868-6810-5414-b79d-ed9c59cf14cc" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eede4f00-fcca-5952-bf0b-1b45f39cc595" :answer/id #uuid "eede4f00-fcca-5952-bf0b-1b45f39cc595" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e1307433-5f5d-5677-8396-c15cc88708bf" :question/id #uuid "e1307433-5f5d-5677-8396-c15cc88708bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-95924" :question/problem "$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Q$ shown above. Find the matrix $R$ such that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of $A.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by ${Q}^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot A & ={Q}^{T}\cdot QR \\ {Q}^{T}\,A & =({Q}^{T}\,Q)R \\ {Q}^{T}\,A & ={I}_{2}R \\ R & ={Q}^{T}\,A\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note that ${Q}^{T}Q={I}_{2}$ since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal.

Now, we calculate the matrix $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ 0 & \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A}
=
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R},
$$

where 

- $Q$ is an $m \times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A),$ and

- $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its diagonal.

For example, the $3\times 2$ matrix

![](images/b7/b71bb9b1dc9aa6d23f2c990052e2e83eeda6000fc64a61ccdb614669d840d38a.svg)

has the QR factorization

![](images/7c/7c5c30e4011efe0ac87f02217dd1f52c6e64658c6e90d22ad8689209badeb1f4.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135097 :tutorial/content "Given the matrix $Q$ in the QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ how do we find $R?$

Recall that $Q$ has orthonormal columns, so pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot A & ={Q}^{T}\cdot QR \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={Q}^{T}QR.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note that since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal we have $Q^TQ = I_n.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}A & =({Q}^{T}Q)R \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={I}_{n}R \\ R & ={Q}^{T}A.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can find $R$ by pre-multiplying $A$ by the transpose of $Q.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135098 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown below:

![](images/ee/ee731d95c111101559ad135429198dd7e0b14313272f0933b1c706006da2fbd2.svg)

Suppose also that we are given the following system of equations that connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A{:}$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

How do we find $R?$
First, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$
![](images/82/824c39c97bb115768856d672b39be8f65d8b4ecbc2ee5d6ccc9f4943594cbacd.svg)

In this new system, the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_1$ correspond to the first-row entries of $R,$ the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_2$ correspond to the second-row entries of $R,$ and the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_3$ correspond to the third-row entries of $R.$ Therefore,

![](images/5b/5ba9887a4d9b47963af171e9275319a2564eca5a4ef8b3ef44978e2ff4b111d9.svg)

To see why this is, we can take the transpose of both sides of $A=QR{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =QR \\ {A}^{T} & =(QR)^{T} \\ {A}^{T} & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T} \\ \overset{{A}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\,\,\,\, & {a}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{{R}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 8 & -4 & 4\end{aligned}]}}\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\,\,\,\, & {q}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{aligned}]}}\end{aligned}

$$
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A}
=
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R},
$$

where 

- $Q$ is an $m \times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A),$ and

- $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its diagonal.

For example, the $3\times 2$ matrix

![](images/b7/b71bb9b1dc9aa6d23f2c990052e2e83eeda6000fc64a61ccdb614669d840d38a.svg)

has the QR factorization

![](images/7c/7c5c30e4011efe0ac87f02217dd1f52c6e64658c6e90d22ad8689209badeb1f4.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135097 :tutorial/content "Given the matrix $Q$ in the QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ how do we find $R?$

Recall that $Q$ has orthonormal columns, so pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot A & ={Q}^{T}\cdot QR \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={Q}^{T}QR.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note that since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal we have $Q^TQ = I_n.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}A & =({Q}^{T}Q)R \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={I}_{n}R \\ R & ={Q}^{T}A.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can find $R$ by pre-multiplying $A$ by the transpose of $Q.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135098 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown below:

![](images/ee/ee731d95c111101559ad135429198dd7e0b14313272f0933b1c706006da2fbd2.svg)

Suppose also that we are given the following system of equations that connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A{:}$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

How do we find $R?$
First, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$

["question-3a08d141-4335-56a2-8562-7ce4a6f3683b" :question/math-academy-id "q-41484"] ["question-3a08d141-4335-56a2-8562-7ce4a6f3683b" :question/problem "$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} & {r}_{13} \\ 0 & {r}_{22} & {r}_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & {r}_{33}\end{aligned}]}}
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. You're given that the system of equations given below connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{2}+6{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

What is the value of ${r}_{11}+{r}_{13}+{r}_{23}?$"] ["question-3a08d141-4335-56a2-8562-7ce4a6f3683b" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ as a linear combination of the vectors ${q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{3}:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{2}+6{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=3{q}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}=-30{q}_{1}+5{q}_{2} \\ {a}_{3}=8{q}_{1}-4{q}_{2}+4{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, this system can be written in matrix form as follows:

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}3 & -30 & 8 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].}}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{r}_{11}+{r}_{13}+{r}_{23}=3+8+(-4)=7.
$$"] ["question-3a08d141-4335-56a2-8562-7ce4a6f3683b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bcc7880c-e1d9-51f3-9d82-55e1eee95989" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

$$

$$\begin{aligned}R=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the QR factorization of $A$ is

$$\overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}] }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] }^{\Large R}.$$"]]}

Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of $q_{11} \cdot r_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ![](images/9c/9c487a6edad04f5c2d192eab5c5cdacbcf3414cbc3c2ea556aca7fa54aec146c.png)

**Step 2**. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-\frac{12}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

![](images/be/be0eeeaf5091163ff418b9c9380a30573e27a7844548e07d8aa4eb89269f39d5.png)

Finally, $q_{11} \cdot r_{12} = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\right) \cdot \left({2\sqrt6}\right) = 2.$"} {:db/id 17592186050578} {:db/id 17592186134324 :question/id #uuid \overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{12}{6})[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & -2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & -2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{12}=(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})\cdot (-2\sqrt{6})=2\sqrt{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186134326 :question/id #uuid "ba99e80b-ab29-52f3-91a8-3caa3a6f75d7" :question/math-academy-id \overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -5 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{9}{9})[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -5 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -5 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{12}=(-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}})\cdot (-3)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$"} {:db/id 17592186364620 :question/id #uuid "5c7952d1-1f1c-50a2-a342-5271912d43de" :question/math-academy-id $$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{31}\cdot {r}_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-(\frac{4}{2})[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{31}\cdot {r}_{12}=(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186395107 :question/id #uuid "1ae0f219-c74d-5218-aeb5-b468ecc59fef" :question/math-academy-id "q-96036" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133798 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "19ae0632-68ac-5da9-8adf-cf71d5ecbc7c" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the QR Factorization of a Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fc8b3e92-0e0d-5d19-bb51-bfe62ab510a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}" :db/id 17592186395109} {:answer/id #uuid "e43f1009-aa53-5355-b6e2-6d08c550cf8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186395110} {:answer/id #uuid "37c89cba-4da8-53a7-87c2-9de05914aaba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}" :db/id 17592186395111} {:answer/id #uuid "56b92eb0-336a-5fcf-8448-085005b2ce34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186395112} {:answer/id #uuid "c551338c-b292-5e26-8b55-ecd82904ce69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186395113}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c551338c-b292-5e26-8b55-ecd82904ce69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186395113} :answer-field/id #uuid "eca9ce0b-73b4-529a-afb7-e8bec3879243" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186395108}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{11}\cdot {r}_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{9}{9})[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{11}\cdot {r}_{12}=(\frac{2}{3})\cdot (-3)=-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186133821 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133633 :question/id #uuid "c6fe3751-c00b-592b-903e-567d95174cd2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5959"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cd18abf3-b551-55d6-a573-690745a65b3e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134352 :question/id #uuid "772d3a4c-3877-5b96-a25a-b75eff00d425" :question/math-academy-id "q-41415"} {:db/id 17592186134354 :question/id #uuid "9fc92fc5-cd9a-5882-b3a5-3c9b7ba00cb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-41417"} {:db/id 17592186363217 :question/id #uuid "9d67166f-3bff-552c-8a7c-19cfbf3fd7f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-140900"} {:db/id 17592186364171 :question/id #uuid "e0bac4d5-3752-5a5d-b6fe-39c8ef101bd9" :question/math-academy-id "q-41485"} {:db/id 17592186364178 :question/id #uuid "0711fb88-caa5-5f45-81df-dbacaf0d183c" :question/math-academy-id "q-41486"} {:db/id 17592186364599 :question/id #uuid "3eed5db2-4721-55a5-93e3-3a839fa38279" :question/math-academy-id "q-95940"} {:db/id 17592186364606 :question/id #uuid "d22b1dfd-700a-5480-96fd-7c46958520e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-95941"} {:db/id 17592186415506 :question/id #uuid "a03feca5-d649-5b96-991d-3e2972b12233" :question/math-academy-id "q-95937"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a QR Factorization of a Matrix Given an Orthogonal Basis in Terms of the Columns of a Matrix"} {:db/id 17592186133633 :question/id #uuid "c6fe3751-c00b-592b-903e-567d95174cd2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5959" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186133821 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cd18abf3-b551-55d6-a573-690745a65b3e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a QR Factorization of a Matrix Given an Orthogonal Basis in Terms of the Columns of a Matrix"}] :question/problem "![](images/3f/3fb28ec29732f0bdc394079d31a08ae597ca1081aed8bb3df0e1219b5fa11a95.png)

$$
{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}={a}_{1} \\ {v}_{2}={a}_{2}-{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{3}={a}_{3}-3{v}_{1}+2{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}

What is the value of $r_{13}+r_{23}+r_{33}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we normalize the vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \mathbin{:}$

$$

Now, the set $\big\{ \mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2,\mathbf{q}_3 \big\}$ will be both orthogonal and normalized.

Next, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$

![](images/2b/2b733751d472729343a3c74af43339f89e9b6142593425d7bf45c912a8f27b4f.png)

![](images/d3/d396c0e50ecbcf618674f01cc24e1c70075be96343138cd8a6d04548b19c5049.png)

Therefore, 

$$
r_{13}+r_{23}+r_{33} = 6+(-6)+4 = 4.

:tutorial/content "Given the matrix $Q$ in the QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ how do we find $R?$

Recall that $Q$ has orthonormal columns, so pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot A & ={Q}^{T}\cdot QR \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={Q}^{T}QR.\end{aligned}$$

Now, note that since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal we have $Q^TQ = I_n.$ Therefore,

$$\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}A & =({Q}^{T}Q)R \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={I}_{n}R \\ R & ={Q}^{T}A.\end{aligned}$$

So, we can find $R$ by pre-multiplying $A$ by the transpose of $Q.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "20b6ab0a-cf41-550b-9242-2bb3f84c4917" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5017 :tutorial/title "Computing the Matrix R Given the Matrix Q in a QR Factorization"} :step/id #uuid "eebb9689-f8b3-55e2-8167-e5f5525e382a" :step/math-academy-id 31388 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134798}} {:db/id 17592186134802 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135098 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown below:

$$\overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}] }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}] }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} & {r}_{13} \\ 0 & {r}_{22} & {r}_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & {r}_{33}\end{aligned}] }^{\Large R}$$

Suppose also that we are given the following system of equations that connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A{:}$

$${\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}$$

How do we find $R?$ First, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$ $${\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad {\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=2{q}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}=-9{q}_{1}+3{q}_{2} \\ {a}_{3}=8{q}_{1}-4{q}_{2}+4{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}$$

In this new system, the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_1$ correspond to the first-row entries of $R,$ the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_2$ correspond to the second-row entries of $R,$ and the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_3$ correspond to the third-row entries of $R.$ Therefore,

$$\overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}] }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}] }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}2 & -9 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] }^{\Large R}.$$

To see why this is, we can take the transpose of both sides of $A=QR{:}$ $$\begin{aligned}A & =QR \\ {A}^{T} & =(QR)^{T} \\ {A}^{T} & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T} \\ \overset{{A}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\,\,\,\, & {a}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{{R}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 8 & -4 & 4\end{aligned}]}}\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\,\,\,\, & {q}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{aligned}]}}\end{aligned}$$

If we were to expand this matrix product, we would obtain our system of equations." :tutorial/id #uuid "9a6d9a3e-33d4-52e8-b8b0-98cd20590dd6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5018 :tutorial/title "Interpreting Relations Between Two Bases as Matrix Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "fdc0053f-e37d-51ef-835e-365ca5c6da98" :step/math-academy-id 31389 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134732}} {:db/id 17592186134803 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135099 :tutorial/content "Let's now go through the QR factorization algorithm to find the factorization of the matrix

$$A = [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}].$$

**Step 1**. Orthogonalize the columns of $A$ to get the columns of $Q.$ Using the Gram-Schmidt process, we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{q}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2**. Compute $R=Q^TA.$ We get

$$\begin{aligned}R=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the QR factorization of $A$ is

$$\overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}] }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ [\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] }^{\Large R}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c2f59e79-8a0c-543b-8af0-381e95a18a8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5019 :tutorial/title "The QR Factorization Algorithm"} :step/id #uuid "94bcb87e-b43a-5740-aaed-1937658ca1d1" :step/math-academy-id 31390 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134799}}] :activity/title "QR Factorization" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134008} {:db/id 17592186134693 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135058 :tutorial/content "The **QR factorization** of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns is the matrix product $$\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A} = \underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R},$$

17592186045417] [17592186046660 1005 17592186046967 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields.
